label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**I'm Going to Explain This Once, Properly**

Jess texted me last night and I've read it about five times, and then I wrote a reply and deleted it three times, because none of the replies were right.

What I keep coming back to isn't the disagreement. It's that she was being kind. She wasn't saying *don't care*. She was saying *care, but not this way, not at this cost*. She's known me long enough — student teaching, 2012, same school, same year, same hallway — to know what I look like when I'm being reckless, and this isn't that. This is something else.

So here's the whole thing in one place, instead of eleven more texts in the group chat where half the people have already made up their minds and the other half are being polite.

---

Last week a parent of one of my students emailed Dr. Halvorsen and cc'd a member of the school committee. Halvorsen forwarded me the thread with one line above it: *Let's talk Thursday.* The email said, and I'm quoting, that the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents."

Thursday is November 19. It's 3:15. It's me, Halvorsen, and her.

Before I say anything else, I want to say this plainly: she's right about the second thing. She is right.

If a kid walks into my classroom and I hand them a recorder and say *ask your grandmother about the buses*, and they feel like the assignment is actually a loyalty test — like the grade depends on what they find out, or like finding out nothing is a failure — then I have put a fifteen-year-old in the position of interrogating their own family. That's a real thing. I don't want to do it. I have never wanted to do it. I don't think she meant it as an attack on the project either. I think she meant it as a warning to me about her kid, and that's the reading I've decided to start from, because it's probably true.

---

Here is what the project actually is, since I don't think I've ever written it down anywhere.

US History II, juniors, two sections. Each student interviews one person about Boston busing and desregation, 1974 through 1976 — ten minutes of recorded conversation, then two pages of reflection. I've run it for four years at Cobb Street. No complaints before this one, and I've never had a single parent ask to opt their kid out.

What I keep, and what I'm adding:

The interview stays. The reflection stays. What I'm adding is a real alternate route, so that no student *has* to interview their own family. They can interview a librarian, a local historian, someone from the NAACP or a community center. Or they can work from the recorded interviews I've collected in previous years — with permission, from the students and the people who were interviewed, which I now have to build in properly instead of treating as a favor. Either way, same ten minutes, same two pages, same reflection prompt: *what did you hear that the textbook doesn't tell you?*

And here's the part I want to say out loud, because I think it was the part that wasn't clear before: **no kid has to interview a family member.** Not if they're not ready. Not if their family doesn't want to talk about it. Not if the project becomes a fight at home. They email me, they do the other thing, and nobody in this building ever hears about it. That's not a concession I'm making under pressure. That's the version of this I should have been running from the start.

---

But here's why I'm not dropping it.

In 2023 a kid — D. — interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in '74. She never told anyone in that family. Not her husband, not her daughters. He sat her down and asked her about the buses and she told him, and he brought it in and played forty seconds of it for the class.

Nobody said a word for about a minute.

Then somebody said, *wait, you drove the bus?* And she — the grandmother, on the recording — said something like *well, I drove the bus and I took my kids to school, and nobody asked me about it before.* And then it was just a normal class period after that, and it was the best forty seconds of teaching I've had.

Last year, a girl found out her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She found out because she interviewed him. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year, and I read a lot of them, because I grade them at night on the couch and complain about it to my wife.

I keep thinking about the second one more than the first, and I want to be careful about why. It's not that I think the girl should have found out that way. She was upset for two days. It's that in the middle of one of those conversations she said, *I didn't know it was like that. I thought it was just — I thought it was something that happened and then everybody moved on.* And I thought: no. It didn't move on. People are still living four blocks from each other. My students are living four blocks from each other. The version of the story where it happened and then everybody moved on is the version the textbook gives you in one paragraph, and the paragraph ends with "tensions eased."

Tensions eased.

I'm sorry. Read the primary sources sometime.

---

Here's the line for me. The kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need it most, and I don't get to force anyone.

Those two things are both true at the same time and I've had to sit with it for four years. There is a version of this where a student is uncomfortable and something in them needs that project — needs the conversation, needs to hear a grandmother say it out loud, needs to understand that the people who did that and the people who were hit by it are both in her family and also both at her school. And there is a version where I push her, and I break something, and I spend three years not being able to teach this kid anything.

So I don't push. I make the room safe. I give her an out she doesn't have to explain. And then I hope the project is still there when she's ready, because I'm not going to drag her to it.

That's the whole moral of it, honestly. That's the line. I've never been able to get further past it than that and I don't think I want to.

---

Now the part where Jess is right again.

I'm tenured, since 2021, and Halvorsen still decides my schedule and still decides who gets AP. She's right that the downside here is real and it's not theoretical. If Thursday goes badly — if the parent wants the project gone and the committee member weighs in — it's not a conversation about one assignment. It's my name in a school committee inbox.

I'm scared. Not performatively. I've been chewing on this for a week. I sat in my car in the driveway on Tuesday and did the math on what I'd have to do next year if I go to the other building, and there is a version of my life where I hate it.

I'm also not going to pretend I'm doing this because I'm brave. I'm doing it because I've read the reflections. I have a drawer file of them, four years' worth, and if you want to know what I think a fifteen-year-old in this city sounds like when she's given the chance to say something true, I will hand you the folder.

---

Jess — I'm not asking you to agree. I think you're right that the smart play is to drop it and do a unit on the textbook paragraph instead. I think most people in the group chat think that's the smart play too, and I don't think any of them are cowards.

But I'd like you to understand why I'm doing it, and I'd like you to understand that I understand why you said what you said.

You taught. You know what a classroom is like at 8:40 on a Tuesday. The difference isn't that you forgot — I promise you haven't. The difference is that from where you are now, the cost of being wrong looks different than it does from inside the building. You left in 2019 and went and did a thing at a biotech in Cambridge that probably pays better and has better hours and doesn't have a parent emailing your principal about your project at 11 at night.

I'm not in Cambridge. I'm in the building, Thursday, 3:15, and there's a recorder in the drawer and a folder of reflections on my desk, and those are the reasons.

This is the history of the city they live in. Not a chapter. Not a unit. The actual history, the kind where somebody's grandmother was on the wrong side of it and nobody in the family ever said so.

---

I'll text you Thursday after the meeting. If it goes well I'll tell you it went well. If it goes badly I'll tell you that too, and I'll probably be a little snippy about it, and you can tell me to get off my case.

Either way: thank you for saying something instead of nothing. And thank you for caring about the job. I do too. That's most of why this is hard.

Go easy on me in the group chat.
